findings.title: eqsolve takes the transitive closure of the 'abstract qualification' congruence, so T == Self, U == Self makes T.X == U.X for two distinct conformances. A tautological fact (Box<X> == Box<X>) is enough to trigger it; baseline and occurs,fixsubst reject

findings.analysis:
solveEquality treats two AssociatedType nodes as congruent when their declarations match, at least one qualification is .abstract, and their qualification types are in the same class. The rule is copied from TypeStore.unifiable(AssociatedType, AssociatedType). For unification it is a binary, non-transitive check. eqsolve applies it inside a union-find, so the classes become transitive:
- (T::P).X is congruent to (Self::P).X through P<T> ~ P<Self>.
- (Self::P).X is congruent to (U::P).X through P<Self> ~ P<U>.
- So (T::P).X and (U::P).X are merged, although both have concrete (where-clause) qualifications that are not abstract.
This is exactly the conclusion that negative/associated-type-inequality.hylo forbids: T and U are equal but have distinct conformances.
The abstract node only has to occur somewhere in the term graph, and node() also adds the children of fact sides. So the trivially true fact Box<X> == Box<X> is enough. The unification-based search can never reach this, because it would need a fact that unifies with the goal; that is why baseline and fixsubst do not accept abs-trans-5.
The deeper problem is the rule itself, which is why abs-trans-2/3 are accepted in every configuration. If v-abs-7 (X == T.X from T == Self, T is P) is valid, then T.X == X == U.X follows by transitivity, contradicting associated-type-inequality. The two rules are inconsistent. soundness.md labels v-abs-7 'valid', but by the negative test's rule it is ill-typed: Self's abstract conformance and T's where-clause conformance are distinct witnesses. Note that the abstract qualification never leaks to callers: member references replace it (abs-launder-2/3 rejected), and bug #3 blocks the paths through T.X in callee signatures (abs-launder.hylo). So the hole is in trait bodies, but there it accepts value conversions between unrelated projections.
findings.suggested_fix: Treat (Self::P).X as an atom keyed by Self's abstract conformance, like every other projection: it is equal to (T::c).X only through a fact, or when c is the abstract witness itself (or a coercion of it). Drop the abstract case from congruent() and from TypeStore.unifiable(AssociatedType, AssociatedType), and turn v-abs-7.hylo into a negative test alongside associated-type-inequality. If v-abs-7 must stay valid, the abstract rule cannot be closed transitively: eqsolve must never merge two classes that each contain a non-abstract projection of the same declaration with different witnesses through an abstract node. Add abs-trans-2/3/5 as negative tests either way.

findings.title: eqsolve's congruence closure is cubic (all-pairs sweeps, one sweep per nesting level, rebuilt for every goal): 14-line program takes 45 s (FIX) / 28.5 s (FULL)
findings.evidence:
perf-alias-7.hylo (14 lines): type G1<Z> = Box<Box<Box<Box<Box<Z>>>>>; type G2<Z> = G1<G1<Z>> ... G7<Z> = G6<G6<Z>>; fun f<U where U == A>() { need<G7<U>, G7<A>>() }
  [BASE] 1 diagnostic ('not enough context to infer a type'), 30 ms
  [FIX]  0 diagnostics, type.user 44915 ms
  [FULL] 0 diagnostics, type.user 28542 ms
perf-alias.hylo (G6, 13 lines): FIX 5655 ms, FULL 3607 ms.
Scaling with literal nesting depth (perf-deep-D.hylo, 6 lines, need<Box^D<U>, Box^D<V>>() under U == V):
  D=50: FIX 179 ms
  D=100: FIX 1397 ms, FULL 893 ms
  D=200: FIX 10939 ms, FULL 7167 ms
That is about 8x per doubling, i.e. cubic.
findings.analysis: node() gives a parent a smaller index than its children, because it appends the parent before recursing. The closure loop is `while changed { for i { for j > i where find(i) != find(j) && congruent(i, j) } }`. Each sweep can therefore only propagate a merge one level up, so a depth-D term needs D sweeps of O(n^2) congruent() calls, each of which projects and casts two types from the TypeStore. That is O(D * n^2) = O(D^3) per goal. Nothing is memoized across goals: every closed equality subgoal rebuilds the graph and the closure from all visible facts. Generic aliases make the blow-up cheap to write, because dealiased() expands G7<U> into a 320-deep term, while unification never expands them.
findings.suggested_fix: Use a standard congruence closure (Downey-Sethi-Tarjan / Nelson-Oppen): a signature table keyed by (constructor, child representatives) plus use-lists and a pending-merge worklist, which is O(n log n). Hash-cons the dealiased terms so that shared subterms are only visited once. Memoize the closed graph per (scope, assumed-fact list), the way canDeriveCoercions memoizes its query.

findings.title: Equality proofs by eqsolve add no depth and no penalty, which changes which conformance resolution selects; programs the baseline rejects are now accepted with a different witness
findings.evidence:
pen-ref-n.hylo: trait P { type X }; Q1 refines P; ... Qn refines Q(n-1); fun f<V, W where W == V, W is Qn>() { given V is P { type X = A }; let z: W.X = A() }
  n=1: BASE 1, FIX 1, FULL 1
  n=2: BASE 1, FIX 0, FULL 0
  n=3: BASE 2, FIX 0, FULL 0
  n=4: BASE 0, FIX 0, FULL 0
Trace of n=2:
  occurs,fixsubst: 'resolve P<W>: 3 layers, 1 done', and the chosen witness is the refinement path (penalty 2).
  occurs,fixsubst,eqsolve: 'resolve P<W>: 3 layers, 2 done, 1 minimal', and the chosen witness is 'penalty 0: $<builtin coercion>($<ConformanceDeclaration at pen-ref-2:7.3>)', the local given coerced through W == V.
findings.analysis: Under search, a derivation of V ~ W costs several BFS layers, and penalties for the facts and built-in symmetry/transitivity givens. Under eqsolve it costs one formThread/match step and adds no penalty. takeSummonResults stops at the first layer that has a result and then ranks by penalty. So candidates that need an equality now finish earlier and cheaper, and the selected conformance (here, which X W.X denotes) changes relative to the baseline. That is consistent with 'lexically closer wins', but it is an elaboration change, not result-preserving, and it moves the threshold at which the two candidates tie. I found no case where it accepts an ill-typed program by itself.
findings.suggested_fix: Decide and document how the size of an equality proof counts toward the 'smallest derivation' order (for example, the number of facts used, plus the penalty of the scope of the farthest fact). Add pen-ref-1..4 to the regression set so the selection rule is pinned.

confirmed.title: eqsolve closes the non-transitive 'abstract qualification' unification rule transitively: T == Self, U == Self yields T.X == U.X for two distinct where-clause conformances; whether it does depends on whether an irrelevant term such as X happens to appear in the term graph
confirmed.evidence:
I re-ran these with eq2-e965a058dfd0/tc-bench and timeout 120.

abs-trans-5 (trait P { type X; fun f<T, U where T == Self, U == Self, T is P, U is P, Box<X> == Box<X>>(x: U.X) { check<T.X>(conv<U.X, T.X>(x)) } }):
- BASE: rc=134, OOM. The baseline does not accept it.
- FIX: 0 diagnostics, 13 ms.
- FULL: 0 diagnostics, 5.5 ms.

abs-trans-4 is the same program without the tautology:
- FIX and FULL: 1 diagnostic, "no coercion from '((U::P).X ~ (T::P).X) ==> ...'".
- BASE: OOM.

The FIX trace shows the elaborated witness: conv<U.X, T.X>($<builtin coercion><(U::P).X, (Self::P).X, (T::P).X>( coercion(refl (U::P).X) )( coercion(refl (Self::P).X) )). That is the chain (U::P).X ~ (Self::P).X ~ (T::P).X, made of two abstract-congruence steps.

abs-trans-2 (need<T.X, U.X>() with fact X == X) and abs-trans-3 (value conversion with fact X == X) give 0 diagnostics under FIX and FULL. They also give 0 under BASE (1.9 s). The BASE trace proof is 'need<T.X, U.X>($<builtin coercion>($14))', where $14 : (Self::P).X ~ (Self::P).X is coerced to T.X ~ U.X by assuming Self ~ T and Self ~ U. So the baseline already reaches the forbidden conclusion when a fact mentions X, and FIX extends it to any graph that merely contains X.

Controls:
- ati.hylo (negative/associated-type-inequality): 1 diagnostic under FIX and FULL.
- v-abs-7.hylo: 0 diagnostics under FIX and FULL.

The conclusion T.X == U.X, with T == U and two distinct where-clause conformances, is exactly what associated-type-inequality.hylo forbids. In addition, adding the always-true fact Box<X> == Box<X> flips rejection into acceptance, so the decision is not a function of the theory.
confirmed.root_cause:
Typer.swift solveEquality, congruent() (around line 5780) copies the rule of TypeStore.unifiable(AssociatedType, AssociatedType) (TypeStore.swift around line 1164). Under that rule, two projections of the same declaration are equal when one qualification is .abstract and the qualification types are equal.

In unification this is a binary, wildcard-like check. Inside the union-find it becomes transitive. (T::$i).X merges with (Self::abstract).X through T ~ Self, and (Self::abstract).X merges with (U::$p).X through U ~ Self. So two non-abstract projections with distinct witnesses land in one class.

The node() function also adds the subterms of every fact, so any fact that mentions X is enough to put the abstract node in the graph. Search needs a fact that unifies with the goal, which is why abs-trans-4 and abs-trans-5 differ.

The underlying rule pair (v-abs-7 valid together with built-in transitivity) is inconsistent with associated-type-inequality. That part is pre-existing: the baseline accepts abs-trans-2/3. eqsolve makes it reachable from trivial facts and cheap. This conflict is not documented in soundness.md, which only lists v-abs-7 as valid.
confirmed.fix:
Option A (cleanest; it is a language decision): an abstract projection (Self::abstract).X is equal only to itself, or to a projection whose witness is the abstract witness or a coercion of it.
- Remove the '.abstract ||' disjunct from congruent() and from TypeStore.unifiable(AssociatedType, AssociatedType).
- Move v-abs-7.hylo to the negative tests next to associated-type-inequality.hylo.
- First run the 192 tests to check that no requirement-signature check relies on the wildcard. Member references already replace the abstract qualification, so they should not.

Option B (keeps v-abs-7 valid and stays order-independent): admit an abstract congruence only when the witness is unique up to the closure. In solveEquality, keep a set `banned: Set<Int>` of abstract nodes and loop:

```swift
repeat {
  reset parent/edges to the fact unions only
  run the closure, where congruent(i, j) returns false for the abstract case
    if the abstract side is in banned
  var newlyBanned = false
  for each abstract AssociatedType node a with declaration D, qualification child q:
    let ws = Set(nodes.indices.filter { n in
      n is a non-abstract AssociatedType of D && find(children[n][0]) == find(q)
    }.map(find))
    if ws.count > 1 && !banned.contains(a) { banned.insert(a); newlyBanned = true }
} while newlyBanned
```

Bans only grow, so the loop terminates and the result is independent of order.

With either option:
- abs-trans-2/3/4/5 are rejected; the concrete projections T.X and U.X stay apart.
- v-abs-7 is accepted under option B, because only one concrete projection exists.
- Add abs-trans-2/3/5 as negative tests.

The search path, match with fixsubst coercions (the baseline proof of abs-trans-2), needs the same guard. That guard only matters for goals with variables, since eqsolve decides closed equality goals.

confirmed.title: eqsolve's congruence closure is cubic in term depth and is rebuilt for every closed equality goal: a 14-line program with generic aliases takes about 45 s (FIX) and 28 s (FULL)
confirmed.evidence:
I re-ran these.

- FIX: 0 diagnostics, type.user 44763 ms.
- BASE: 1 diagnostic ('not enough context to infer a type'), 30.7 ms.
- The attacker measured FULL at 28.5 s.

- The attacker measured D=200 at 10.9 s (FIX) and 7.2 s (FULL), about 8x per doubling.

The result itself is correct: the program is valid, and the baseline's rejection was incompleteness. Only the time is the problem.
confirmed.root_cause:
Typer.swift solveEquality, closure loop:

```swift
while changed { for i in nodes.indices { for j in nodes.indices where j > i && find(i) != find(j) && congruent(i, j) { ... } } }
```

node() appends a parent before recursing into its children, so parents have smaller indices than children. One sweep therefore propagates a merge only one level upward. A depth-D term needs D sweeps of O(n^2) congruent() calls, and each call does TypeStore subscripts and existential casts. That is O(D*n^2), about O(D^3) for nested terms.

Nothing is cached. Every closed equality subgoal re-collects the facts, rebuilds the graph (dealiasing generic aliases to exponential depth relative to the source) and recloses it.
confirmed.fix:
Replace the all-pairs fixpoint with a standard congruence closure (Downey-Sethi-Tarjan / Nelson-Oppen):
- Keep `useList: [[Int]]`, the parents of each class representative.
- Keep a signature table `[Signature: Int]`, where Signature = (constructor kind plus its non-child attributes: TypeApplication arity, Arrow style/effect/labels/access, RemoteType access, AssociatedType declaration, ...) together with the find() of the children.
- Keep a pending worklist of pairs to merge.
- On union(x, y): for each parent p in the smaller class's use list, recompute its signature. If the table already holds q with an equal signature and find(q) != find(p), push (p, q) with a congruence edge. Then concatenate the use lists.

This is O(n log n) and removes the per-level sweeps. Even a minimal patch, iterating i and j in descending index order so that children are processed before parents, removes the factor D in the common case.

Also:
- Memoize the closed graph per (scopeOfUse, environment.givens) so that the subgoals of one resolution reuse it.
- Hash-cons dealiased(x) so that shared alias expansions are visited once.

If finding 1's option B is adopted, its abstract-node check must also run per merge rather than as an all-pairs pass.

rejected.title: Equality proofs by eqsolve add no depth and no penalty, which changes which conformance resolution selects (pen-ref-n.hylo)
rejected.why:
It reproduces, but it is not a defect by the task's definitions.

Results (diagnostics, BASE / FIX / FULL):
- pen-ref-1: 1 / 1 / 1.
- pen-ref-2: 1 / 0 / 0.
- pen-ref-3: 2 / 0 / 0.
- pen-ref-4: 0 / 0 / 0.

Both candidates for P<W> are legitimate witnesses: the where-clause refinement path, and the local given coerced through the fact W == V. The FIX trace reports '2 done, 1 minimal', so there is no tie and no ambiguity is hidden. The selected witness has the right type. The baseline already shows the same threshold behaviour, just at n=4.

So the configuration accepts more programs through a valid derivation. That is not unsoundness, not a regression and not order dependence.

I also tried the mirror case to see whether FIX would now reject something the baseline accepts. In mirror-0/1/2.hylo in /home/user/hylo-new/research/round3/soundness/review2/eq-unsound-judge/, the where-clause conformance V is P is reached through W == V, and the competitor is a local given of a refining trait. findings.title: eqsolve + fixsubst make an inferred generic argument ambiguous when it is fixed only by an equality chain (valid call rejected)
findings.analysis: The premises are discharged last-first, so the open equality A0 ~ ?u is solved before Q<?u>. eqsolve does not apply to open goals, so the search runs with fixsubst. That search now produces several bindings in the same layer: ?u := A1 (fact), ?u := A2 (the fact A1 ~ A2 by coercion; fixsubst keeps ?u := A2, then eqsolve proves A1 ~ A0 in one step at penalty 0), and ?u := A0 (reflexivity). Each then reaches Q<?u> by coercing the single conformance A2 is Q, and eqsolve proves that equality in one step at penalty 0 too. In the baseline the coercion paths needed symmetry/transitivity steps, so they finished later than the direct derivation and only one result survived. All the competing results use the same conformance and pick U among types that are equal in the theory, so the ambiguity is spurious. Two side notes: Sequence.minimalElements (Utilities/Sequence+Extensions.swift) keeps later non-minimal elements once two leaves tie, which is why '4 minimal' is printed with penalties 1,1,3,5. That bug is pre-existing, but eqsolve hits it more often.
findings.suggested_fix: For an open equality goal whose one side is a bare unification variable, return only the most general solution (bind the variable to the other side, i.e. reflexivity) instead of searching. Every other solution is equal to it modulo the closure, and later goals such as Q<A0> are discharged through coercion plus eqsolve. More generally, treat results whose witnesses differ only by types equal under the congruence closure as one result. Fix minimalElements so that it keeps only the minimal elements. Add o2b, o2 and o2d as positive tests.

findings.title: extorder reports a false 'circular extension' on a conditional extension whose where clause mentions an associated type with the same name as one of its members
findings.analysis: In resolve(_:declaredIn:...), extorder reports a circular extension whenever the lookup of a name n meets an extension that declares n and is on declarationsOnStack. This holds whatever type the lookup is in and whether or not that extension could apply to it. While E's extendee is computed, its where clause or extendee path looks up 'Element' in a rigid generic parameter T, or in an unrelated nominal type (List, A). E declares 'Element', so the error fires. Yet E (extending Box<T>, Wrapper<...> or List.Node) can never apply to T or List. Even under the 'apply if consistent' reading, the only consistent answer is that E does not apply. Both language options proposed in soundness.md accept these programs: (a) a pre-pass for extendees that ignores extension members, and (b) a fixpoint. The baseline's silent skip gives the right answer here. The pattern is ordinary code: a conditional extension constrained on T.Element that defines its own Element, or a nested type extended with a same-named alias.
findings.suggested_fix: Report a circular extension only when e could apply to the type being looked up, judged without e's extendee: compare the head constructor of e's extendee syntax, or its nominal root after resolving only non-extension members, with the queried type. Never report it for lookups in a generic parameter or associated type unless e is a blanket extension ('extension <T ...> T'). Alternatively, resolve extendees in a pre-pass that ignores extension members, option (a), and keep the error for genuinely mutual cases such as n02-n04. Add x10b, x01, x03 and x09 as positive tests.

findings.title: eqsolve proofs carry no penalty, which breaks the scope-based preference between derivations (valid program rejected as ambiguous)
findings.analysis: In summon, eqsolve's .proved branch calls formThread(... penalties: penalties) and adds no group offset for the facts used. The search adds 'penalties + grouping.offset' for every given it uses, including the equality facts and the built-ins. Two derivations that the baseline separates by the scope distance of the equality fact therefore tie under FIX. They also finish in the same layer, because eqsolve takes one step.
findings.suggested_fix: Give the eqsolve proof a penalty computed from the facts it uses: the group offset of each fact edge in givens(visibleFrom:) order, plus the assumed givens' offsets. Choose the path by a minimum-cost search (Dijkstra over the edge offsets) rather than BFS. That way closer equalities keep winning as they did with the search.

findings.title: eqsolve silently changes the selected conformance witness (different elaboration, not visible in --dump)
findings.evidence:
Program: f<A, B where B == A>, with nested scopes. In k: 'given A is R'. In h: 'given B is P', 'given <where A is Q> => A is P', 'given <where A is R> => A is Q', and the call g<A>().
All configurations: 0 diagnostics, and semtest reports the dumps as identical.
Trace, baseline: 'resolve [Void]() let -> Void: 4 layers, 2 done, 1 minimal  penalty 1: g<A>($<Conf 11.7>($<Conf 12.7>($<Conf 8.5>)))', which uses the conditional chain through A is R.
Trace, FIX: '4 layers, 2 done, 1 minimal  penalty 0: g<A>($<builtin coercion>($<Conf 10.7>))', which uses B is P transported along B == A.
findings.analysis: This has the same cause as the penalty finding. The derivation through the outer-scope equality fact cost the baseline 2 (its conformance offset 0 plus the fact's offset 2) against 1 for the chain. Under eqsolve it costs 0, so FIX picks a different conformance witness. That conformance has different implementations, so runtime behaviour can change without any diagnostic. The --dump oracle cannot see the change, because it records only expression types and name references, not witnesses. The claim that FIX is dump-identical therefore does not cover the choice of witness.
findings.suggested_fix: The penalty fix above. Also extend the oracle to dump the elaborated implicit arguments (the witness expressions), so that a change of selection is caught.

findings.title: eqsolve congruence closure is cubic and is rebuilt for every equality goal: 34-line program takes 10 s (FIX) / 5.6 s (FULL)
findings.evidence:

findings.analysis: For every closed equality goal, solveEquality rebuilds the term graph from all the visible facts. It then closes it with a naive fixpoint ('while changed { for i, j in nodes ... congruent(i, j) }'), which costs O(passes · n²) TypeStore projections. Nothing is memoized per scope or set of givens. Every equality subgoal that a conformance search raises pays the full cost again. It is still far better than the baseline, which runs out of memory, but it exceeds the 5 s budget on a short (if wide) program.
findings.suggested_fix: Use a standard congruence closure: a signature table or use-lists with a pending queue, O(n log n). findings.title: A given whose type is being computed is silently skipped, so FIX accepts an ambiguous program and the result depends on declaration order (alias memoized through the skip)
findings.analysis:
This is the remaining silent skip, lens (3).
1. The checker computes the declared type of G1 ('given Z.O is P'), which evaluates the alias Z = T.Y.
2. That evaluation looks up Y on T through the trait P, so it calls summon(P<T>).
3. givens(visibleFrom:) filters G1 out with notOnStack, so only G2 ('T is P { Y = U }') is found, and Z := U.
4. The summon result itself is not memoized (hasImplicitOnStack guards it). The alias type Z is memoized as U, permanently.
5. G1's type then becomes P<(U::Q).O>, and summon treats that as P<T>. So T has two conformances to P, and T.Y is ambiguous. Z = U is therefore not a consistent reading: the program has no consistent reading and should be rejected.

In the other order (gz3), Z is evaluated first and the self-reference is detected, so the program is rejected. Swapping two adjacent top-level declarations changes acceptance.

extorder replaced the silent skip of on-stack extensions with an error, but the identical silent skip of on-stack givens (notOnStack in givens(visibleFrom:)) is untouched. Every value memoized during that window that is not a summon result can be wrong: alias types, extendees, declared types.

How to reach it: a value context parameter ('let v: X') in a given's implication becomes an assumed given whose type is a bare variable ?x. Pending premises stay in environment.givens while later premises are proven (discharge is last-first), so $1 : ?x is a candidate witness for the premise Box<?x>.   type D4<T> = D3<D3<D3<D3<T>>>>

findings.analysis: solveEquality rebuilds the whole term graph for each closed equality subgoal and closes it with `while changed { for i in nodes { for j in nodes where j > i ... congruent(i,j) } }`. node() appends a parent before its children, so the outer constructors get lower indices. Each pass then merges only one more level of a nested pair: the inner pair becomes congruent only after the pass has already visited the outer pairs. A depth-d goal therefore needs d passes of O(n^2) congruent() calls, each doing two existential type-store projections: O(d·n^2) = O(n^3). Generic aliases make n exponential in the number of source lines. Nothing is cached across subgoals.
findings.suggested_fix: Use a standard congruence closure: a signature table plus use-lists (Nelson-Oppen or Downey-Sethi-Tarjan, O(n log n)). Or at least process candidate pairs bottom-up and re-examine only the parents of merged classes. Memoize the closure per (scope, assumed-equality set), since facts rarely change between subgoals. Bound the term size or fall back to notApplicable above a limit.

confirmed.title: eqsolve congruence closure is cubic: a 10-line program takes 22.7 s (FIX) / 14.6 s (FULL)
confirmed.evidence: Re-run p3: FIX 'diagnostics: 0, type.user 22689 ms'. FULL 'diagnostics: 0, type.user 14634 ms'. Baseline: 29 ms, rejecting with 'not enough context to infer a type'. Scaling under FIX: p1-deep-25 30.9 ms, p1-deep-50 176 ms, p1-deep-100 1447 ms (about 8x per doubling, so cubic). p2 (depth 128) 2987 ms. One more alias level would go far beyond 120 s.
confirmed.root_cause: In solveEquality (Typer.swift ~5795-5816), the closure loop is `while changed { for i in nodes { for j in nodes where j > i && find(i) != find(j) && congruent(i, j) {...} } }`. Each pass is O(n^2) congruent() calls, each doing type-store projections. node() numbers parents before children, so a pass merges only one more level of a nested pair, and d nesting levels need d passes: O(d*n^2) = O(n^3). The graph is rebuilt from scratch for every closed equality subgoal, and generic aliases make n large relative to the source size.
confirmed.fix: Replace the fixpoint loop with standard congruence closure (Downey-Sethi-Tarjan / Nelson-Oppen): a signature table keyed by (constructor tag, find(children)), plus use-lists. On each union, re-canonicalise only the parents of the merged class's members, processed through a worklist; this is O(n log n). Cheaper interim fix: iterate pairs bottom-up (children before parents, i.e. reverse node order) so that one pass suffices for pure nesting, and hash nodes by signature instead of comparing all pairs. Also memoize the closed graph per (scope, set of fact givens), and give up (notApplicable) above a node-count cap.

confirmed.title: Arrow environments are invisible to hasVariable, so eqsolve treats an open goal as closed and refutes it (valid program rejected; baseline accepted)
confirmed.evidence: Re-run: baseline 'diagnostics: 0'. FIX and FULL: 1 diagnostic, "no coercion from '<X, Y> (X ~ Y) ==> ...' to '[Void](let [E](let Void) let -> Void, let [%6pv](let Void) let -> Void) let -> Void'". The program is valid with ?e := E. With an explicit type argument (/home/user/hylo-new/research/round3/soundness/review2/crash-paths-judge/a4-explicit.hylo, mk<E>()) or an annotated let (a4-annot.hylo), FIX accepts. This is the same root cause and also leaves unreified variables in accepted elaborations.
confirmed.root_cause: Arrow.properties omits environment.properties, so `goal[.hasVariable]` is false for [E](..) ~ [?e](..). solveEquality then treats the goal as closed, makes ?e an opaque leaf and refutes it, while search would have bound ?e := E by reflexivity. The same blind bit makes reify skip such arrows (free variables in elaborations) and lets summon memoize goals that contain variables.
confirmed.fix: The same fix as the environment-cycle crash: include environment.properties in Arrow.properties. As defence in depth until then, solveEquality could determine closedness by walking the goal itself instead of trusting `[.hasVariable]`.

rejected.title: Congruence of abstract-qualified associated types identifies Self.X with U.X for a distinct conformance 'U is P' (e2)
rejected.why: It reproduces: e2 is accepted by baseline, FIX and FULL, and e3 is rejected by all three. But this is not a defect of the configuration under test. It is not an unsoundness or regression introduced by FIX or FULL.

findings.title: eqsolve recomputes a cubic congruence closure of every equality in scope for each equality goal, even trivially reflexive ones: 26-line valid program takes 52 ms on the baseline and 14.5 s under FULL
findings.evidence:
Runner: /home/user/hylo-new/research/round3/soundness/review2/perf/run.py <base|fix|full> file (python wrapper: timeout, --count, wall time, maxrss). The family has where-clauses T == U, X1 == Box^10<T>, Y1 == Box^10<U>, ..., Xk == Box^10<X(k-1)>, Yk == Box^10<Y(k-1)>, and m reflexive goals need<Box^j<T>, Box^j<T>>().
cc-refl-k16-w10-m4 (26 lines): base 52.6 ms; FULL 14467 ms (counters: eqsolve.proved=8 summon.matches=16, so all the time is inside solveEquality).
cc-refl-k12-w10-m8 (26 lines): base 68 ms (summon.matches=768); FULL 12283 ms (eqsolve.proved=8, summon.matches=16).
Scaling in k at m=1, FULL: k4 60 ms, k8 448 ms, k16 3667 ms. That is about 8x per doubling, so cubic. Base stays at 17-35 ms. The cost is linear in the number of distinct goals.
With non-reflexive goals (cc-chain-kK-w10-m1, need<Xk, Yk>): k24 (31 lines) takes 12.3 s under FULL and 19.5 s under FIX; base runs out of memory after 35 s (bogus-derivation search). cc-chain-k16-w10-m8 (30 lines): FULL 31.2 s; base out of memory.
Deep facts plus distinct goals: cc-deep-60-m30 (34 lines) takes 11.4 s under FULL.
findings.analysis: solveEquality (Typer.swift, eqsolve) is called from summon for every closed equality goal. It rebuilds the whole term graph from all equality givens in scope, then closes it with `while changed { for i in nodes { for j > i where find(i) != find(j) && congruent(i, j) ... } }`. node() assigns an index to a parent before its children, so parents have lower indices. A scan in index order therefore merges only one more level of nesting per round. A fact set of depth d with n nodes needs about d rounds of O(n^2) congruent() calls (each is a TypeStore lookup plus existential casts), which is O(n^3) per goal. Nothing is memoized across goals, although in one scope the facts are identical for every goal. Goals that the baseline proves in one reflexivity match (need<T, T>) pay the full closure. Only a fact set built from nested structured sides triggers this. Atom-only equalities are cheap.
findings.suggested_fix: (1) Fast path: if the dealiased sides are identical, return reflexivityWitness without building the graph. (2) Replace the pairwise fixpoint with a standard congruence closure (signature table plus use-lists, Downey-Sethi-Tarjan / Nelson-Oppen). That is O(n log n) and merges parents once their children merge. (3) Memoize the closed graph per (scope, assumed equality givens) and only add the goal's nodes incrementally, as cache.scopeToSummoned already does for results. (4) Add eqsolve.nodes and eqsolve.rounds counters so the cost is visible.

findings.title: occurs check is exponential on DAG-shaped substitutions: 13-line valid program takes 20 ms on the baseline, 14 s under FIX and 10.7 s under FULL
findings.evidence:
Program: given <A0..A24> => Foo<{A24, A23, ..., A0}, {Bar, P<A24,A24>, ..., P<A1,A1>}, Baz> is R; given <Z where Foo<Z, Z, Bar> is R> => Bar is Q; given <where Bar is S> => Bar is Q; given Bar is S; need<Bar>(). It is valid through the second route. The first route builds the DAG and then fails on Baz vs Bar.
occurs-valid-20: base 20 ms, FULL 698 ms. occurs-valid-22: base 20 ms, FULL 2669 ms. occurs-valid-24: base 20.4 ms, FIX 14072 ms, FULL 10734 ms. All accept (diagnostics: 0).
Isolated: occurs-only-18 (the same without the valid route, rejected in every configuration): base 20 ms, flags 'occurs' alone 444 ms, FULL 346 ms. occurs-only-22: base 22 ms, FULL 5430 ms. occurs-only-24 (10 lines, one line of 559 columns): base 21 ms, FULL 21260 ms. That is 4x per +2, so 2^n.
Related pre-existing blowup on the success path: occurs-dag-18 (9 lines, valid) takes 13.4 s on base, 12.0 s with 'occurs', 11.7 s under FIX and 8.9 s under FULL. occurs-dag-16: base 3.1 s, FULL 2.1 s. reify is also unmemoized on the DAG.
findings.analysis: Unifying the premise Foo<?z, ?z, Bar> with the head works left to right. It first binds ?z to the tuple of variables. It then unifies that tuple with {Bar, P<?a24,?a24>, ...}, which binds ?a24 := Bar, ?a23 := P<?a24,?a24>, ?a22 := P<?a23,?a23>, and so on. That is a DAG in the local SubstitutionTable. TypeStore.occurs(v, in: t, under: ss) dereferences ss[t] and recurses into every child with no visited set. The `!u[.hasVariable]` early exit tests the syntactic type, which still has variables after they are bound. Each new binding therefore walks the whole shared DAG as a tree, 2^(n-k) nodes, for 2^n in total. The baseline has no occurs check, so on a failing candidate it never walks the DAG. That candidate is an alternative tried in the same BFS layer as the successful one, so a valid program pays the cost.
findings.suggested_fix: Make occurs linear: carry a set of variables (or type identities) already proven not to contain v during one check, or check only variable-to-variable edges with a visited set on the substitution graph. Memoize reify(…, applying:) per call on DAG-shaped tables as well, which fixes the pre-existing occurs-dag blowup. Add occurs-valid-N and occurs-dag-N to the perf regression set.

findings.title: A single unrelated equality in scope turns off absmodel and the index: a 9-line valid overloaded call runs out of memory under FULL, but takes 3 ms without the equality
findings.evidence:
Program: three looping givens <T where Si<T> is P> => T is P; fun h<T where T is P>(x: T) {}; fun h(x: Yb) {}; fun f<A, B where A == B>() { h(Yb()) }. Valid: the second overload applies.
div-eq-ovl-b3-1: base out of memory ('failed to allocate', exit -6) after 50.9 s; FIX out of memory after 53.3 s; FULL out of memory after 35.3 s (maxrss 1862 MB).
div-eq-ovl-b3-0 (identical without 'where A == B'): FULL 3.17 ms, summon.matches=1, absmodel.refuted=4.
b=2: div-eq-ovl-b2-1 takes 1086 ms under FULL (absmodel.inconclusive=1, index.fallback=3072, summon.matches=112129); div-eq-ovl-b2-0 takes 3.8 ms under FULL.
The same holds for the rejected div-eq-b3-1 (FULL out of memory after 35 s) against div-eq-b3-0 (FULL 2.7 ms).
findings.analysis: In AbstractResolution.add, any clause whose head is an equality sets isInconclusive. A ground where-clause given A ~ B is such a clause, so the model built for f's scope (and all its sub-scopes) refutes nothing. indexedSummon also falls back whenever ix.coercionSources is non-empty. Inside any generic function with an equality requirement, FULL therefore reverts to the baseline's exponential search on divergent givens (README §4: div-branch is exponential in the cap). The candidate h<T where T is P> is tried during overload resolution, so a valid program pays for the failing branch. The FULL configuration's protection against divergent search disappears exactly in the code that eqsolve was meant to serve.
findings.suggested_fix: Keep the model conclusive under ground equality givens. Over-approximate by quotienting with the eqsolve classes: abstract every type in a non-trivial class (and any type with an abstract-qualified associated type) to ⊤ or to the class representative before building clauses and queries. Do the same for indexedSummon, which can use the class representative as its key. Equality goals themselves stay unrefuted by the model, as today.

findings.title: Open-variable equality goals are still searched with symmetry and transitivity: a 3-line valid program runs out of memory in every configuration, and a 3-line ill-typed one takes 24 s under FULL
findings.evidence:
open-wide-k: fun pick<T, U1..Uk where Ui is Q, T == Ui>(x: T) {}; fun f<A0 where A0 is Q>(x: A0) { pick(x) }. Valid with Ui := A0.
k=1: base 33 ms, FULL 6 ms. k=2: base 133 ms, FULL 54 ms (3932 matches). k=3: base 3.8 s (154k matches), FULL 2.4 s (141693 matches, eqsolve.proved=389). k=4: base out of memory after 37.6 s, FIX out of memory after 38.5 s, FULL out of memory after 27.1 s.
open-neg-0 (3 lines, ill-typed: fun f<A0>(x: A0) { pick(x) } with a single U): base out of memory after 35 s; FIX 31.4 s (1268905 matches); FULL 24.0 s (1205345 matches, eqsolve.proved=6575, maxrss 1.6 GB). FULL by cap: cap 6 5.5k matches / 79 ms, cap 8 72k / 1.2 s, cap 10 1.2M / 24 s, about 16x per +2 on the cap. open-neg-1 (one equality A0 == A1 added): FULL out of memory after 29.5 s.
findings.analysis: Premises are discharged last-in, first-out, so A0 ~ ?u is attempted while ?u is still open. solveEquality returns notApplicable when the goal has variables. summon then tries every assumed given, every visible given (including the stdlib's) and reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity. transitivity<A0, ?e, ?u> creates further open equality goals at each layer. The branching is unbounded up to the depth cap, and absmodel cannot refute equalities (mayDerive returns true for the equality key). This is pre-existing: the baseline also runs out of memory. eqsolve does not cover it, though the design note in soundness.md §2 says open goals should be handled.
findings.suggested_fix: In solveEquality, handle open goals whose facts are all ground: (a) when one side is a bare variable, enumerate the members of the other side's congruence class, plus the side itself, as candidate bindings, giving one thread each with the path proof; (b) otherwise unify syntactically and check the residual pairs against the closure. Never fall back to transitivity search with open middle variables. At minimum, do not offer transitivity or symmetry for goals with an open side when no equality given is in scope. Discharging premises in forward order (also needed for bug #3) would bind U through 'U is Q' first in most of these programs.

findings.title: Branching divergence that absmodel cannot refute (div-branch-trunc generalized): 14 lines take 11 s under FULL, and 16 lines run out of memory
findings.evidence:
div-trunc-bN: N pairs of (struct Si<T>; given <T where Si<T> is P> => T is P; given Si<Si<Xi>> is P) and need<where Yb is P>() (underivable).
b1: FULL 3.5 ms (39 matches). b2: FULL 212 ms (6137 matches); base 1.7 s (112k matches). b3 (14 lines): FULL 11265 ms (236191 matches, index.skipped=7.9M, maxrss 587 MB); base out of memory after 53 s; FIX out of memory after 55.6 s. b4 (17 lines): FULL out of memory after 32 s; FIX out of memory after 45 s.
findings.analysis: The facts Si<Si<Xi>> is P truncate at k=2 to P(Si(Si(⊤))), so the model derives P(⊤) for every branch and prunes nothing. BFS then explores about b^(cap/2) distinct subgoals. This is the documented limitation of absmodel (README §4.3), but with b=3 it crosses 5 s and with b=4 it crashes under FULL. FULL is 5-50x better than base and FIX, yet still pathological.
findings.suggested_fix: As README §4.4 recommends: a global match budget per resolution (fail with a 'resolution too complex' diagnostic instead of running out of memory), and a per-thread height bound instead of the BFS step cap. Alternatively, make the model's truncation keep the exact ground facts so that P(⊤) is not derived from them (for example, k-depth with ground facts stored untruncated for refutation).

confirmed.title: TypeStore.occurs walks DAG-shaped substitutions as trees, so it is exponential (13-line valid program: base 22 ms, FULL 10.9 s)
confirmed.evidence: Re-run. occurs-valid-24 base: diagnostics 0, 22.4 ms, 223 matches. FULL: diagnostics 0, 10868 ms, summon.matches=5. With the flag 'occurs' alone, occurs-only-22 takes 7105 ms (1 diagnostic, correctly rejected; the attacker reports base at 22 ms). Related pre-existing case occurs-dag-16: base 3054 ms, FULL 2354 ms. That cost is in reify, not occurs, and the baseline has it too.
confirmed.root_cause: TypeStore.swift occurs(_:in:under:) (about lines 1082-1105) is called from both variable cases of unifiable (lines 1008/1012) on every binding. It dereferences ss[t] and recurses into all children with no memo. `!u[.hasVariable]` tests the syntactic type, and that type still has variables after they are bound in ss. Unifying the premise with the head binds ?a23 := P<?a24,?a24>, ?a22 := P<?a23,?a23>, and so on, which is a shared DAG. Each check walks 2^k paths. The baseline has no occurs check, so it never pays this on the failing alternative, which sits in the same BFS layer as the successful one.
confirmed.fix: Make occurs linear for one call. Thread a `var clean: Set<AnyTypeIdentity>` through a private recursive helper. Return false right away for a type already in `clean`, and insert u after its children are found variable-free of v. ss is not mutated during the call, so this is exact. Optionally also skip a variable that has already been dereferenced. The cost becomes O(size of the DAG) per binding. Separately, memoize reify(_:applying:) by type identity within one call. confirmed.title: Open-variable equality goals are not handled by eqsolve and fall back to unbounded symmetry/transitivity search: 3-line valid program OOMs in every configuration; 3-line ill-typed program takes 24 s and 1.6 GB under FULL
confirmed.evidence: Re-run. open-wide-4 (valid): FULL 'failed to allocate' exit -6 after 26.7 s (maxrss 1879 MB); FIX OOM after 37.9 s; base OOM after 37.5 s. open-neg-0 (ill-typed, a single 'T == U, U is Q'): FULL 24031 ms, 1 correct diagnostic, summon.matches=1205345, eqsolve.proved=6575, maxrss 1612 MB; base OOM after 34.9 s. This is pre-existing: the baseline is no better, and FIX/FULL are not worse.
confirmed.root_cause: threadContinuation discharges premises last-in, first-out, so `T ~ ?U` is posed while ?U is still open. solveEquality returns .notApplicable as soon as the reified goal has a variable (`if goal[.hasVariable] ... return .notApplicable`). summon then offers reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity<A0, ?e, ?U> and every visible equality given. Each transitivity step creates new open equality goals, so the branching is bounded only by the depth cap. absmodel never refutes equality goals. soundness.md section 2 requires the procedure to handle open goals, and the implementation does not.
confirmed.fix: In solveEquality, after collecting facts, handle open goals when every fact is ground. Minimal, complete case: if `facts` is empty, the only derivable equalities are syntactic identities modulo aliases and the abstract associated-type rule. Return a new case `.unify(SubstitutionTable)` holding the result of program.types.unifiable(lhs, rhs) under environment.substitutions, or .refuted when they do not unify. summon then forms exactly one thread that binds the variables and uses reflexivityWitness, and offers no symmetry or transitivity. General case with facts: if one side is a bare variable, return one candidate thread per node in the other side's class (path proof as for ground goals). Otherwise unify syntactically and check the residual pairs against the closure. Never return to transitivity search with an open middle variable. Validate inferred bindings and ambiguity with semtest, since this is rigid E-unification and can change which bindings are found. Discharging premises in forward order (needed for bug #3 anyway) would also bind U through 'U is Q' first in these programs.

confirmed.title: Any ground equality given in scope makes absmodel inconclusive and disables the index, so divergent givens explode again: 9-line valid overloaded call OOMs under FULL (3 ms without the where-clause)
confirmed.evidence: Re-run. div-eq-ovl-b3-1 FULL: 'Fatal error: failed to allocate 411041712 bytes', exit -6 after 35.6 s, maxrss 1862 MB. div-eq-ovl-b3-0 (the same program without 'where A == B') FULL: diagnostics 0, 3.18 ms, absmodel.refuted=4, summon.matches=1. div-eq-ovl-b2-1 FULL: 1133 ms, absmodel.inconclusive=1, index.fallback=3072, summon.matches=112129. b2-0 FULL: 3.13 ms. This is pre-existing: the attacker reports that base and FIX also OOM, and FIX has no absmodel. It is a real performance hole in FULL's protection, triggered by the very feature (equality requirements) that eqsolve was built for.
confirmed.root_cause: AbstractResolution.swift add(_:) sets `isInconclusive = true` for any clause with an `.equality` head (lines 102-108). The where-clause given A ~ B of f is such a clause, so f's scope model (and every sub-scope model) refutes nothing. indexedSummon (Typer.swift line 4208) also returns nil whenever ix.coercionSources is non-empty. Under FULL, a generic function with any equality requirement therefore falls back to the baseline's exponential search on divergent givens, and overload resolution tries the failing candidate h<T where T is P>. (REPORT.md documents the inconclusive-on-equality rule; soundness.md does not.)
confirmed.fix: When eqsolve is on and every equality given in scope is ground (the same test solveEquality uses for its fact list), keep the model conclusive by quotienting. Compute the eqsolve closure classes once per scope. In abstraction(of:), map to ⊤ every type whose node lies in a class of size > 1, and every associated type with an abstract qualification whose qualification type is in such a class. Then add the clauses with the equality-headed clause dropped instead of marking the model inconclusive. Conformance facts and queries that could be related through coercion along A ~ B then both contain ⊤ at that position and still unify. That is a sound over-approximation, because without decomposition every derivable equality lies inside the closure. Keep `mayDerive` returning true for equality goals, and keep the inconclusive fallback when a quantified or conditional equality given is present. Do the same in indexedSummon: key on the class representative, or keep falling back only when the goal mentions a class member.

confirmed.title: Branching divergence that absmodel cannot refute (div-branch-trunc generalized): 14-line ill-typed program takes 11.3 s under FULL; 17 lines OOM
confirmed.evidence: Re-run. FULL: 1 correct diagnostic, 11345 ms, summon.matches=236191, index.skipped=7912499, maxrss 587 MB. FIX: OOM ('failed to allocate', exit -6) after 37.9 s. The attacker reports that base also OOMs and that b4 OOMs under FULL. This is pre-existing and the known absmodel limitation of README section 4.3 (div-branch-trunc). It is not caused by the fixes, but it meets the >5 s / crash criterion.
confirmed.root_cause: Depth-2 truncation turns the facts Si<Si<Xi>> is P into P(Si(Si(⊤))), and the looping clauses <T where Si<T> is P> => T is P then derive P(⊤), so the model cannot refute P(Yb). BFS with a size cap of 10 explores about b^(cap/2) distinct subgoals and has no memory or work budget. That ends in an allocation failure instead of a diagnostic.
confirmed.fix: Add a global per-resolution budget on summon.matches (or live threads) in summon/resolve. When it is exhausted, stop and report a 'implicit resolution too complex' diagnostic instead of growing the frontier until allocation fails. Separately, let the model refute these goals: store ground facts untruncated in an `exact` set, and derive truncated facts only from clause applications. Alternatively use a type-directed depth (k proportional to the maximum fact depth plus 1), so that Si<Si<Xi>> does not collapse to ⊤ before the loop.

confirmed.title: Return-type overloads are exponential in the argument count under FIX and FULL (10-line valid program: FULL 8.3 s); the existing 'solver' flag that fixes it is not in the configuration
confirmed.evidence: Re-run. FULL: diagnostics 0, 8292 ms, coerced.slowPath=304569, summon.matches=304569. FIX: 11070 ms. base: 10375 ms. FULL+solver: 3.62 ms, coerced.slowPath=27, summon.matches=27, diagnostics 0. This is pre-existing and unrelated to the semantic fixes.
confirmed.root_cause: Each h() overload forks the constraint system (4^n forks). Each fork's argument mismatch goes through the slow path of coerced(), one implicit resolution per fork. Neither FIX nor FULL prunes overloads by the expected parameter type before forking.
confirmed.fix: Add 'solver' to FULL after a semtest run against the baseline on the 192 tests and 24 workloads. Or, in the solver, filter overload candidates by whether their result type unifies with the known parameter type (cheap syntactic check) before forking, and run coerced() only for candidates that survive.

rejected.title: (none rejected outright) Notes on scope of findings 3-6
rejected.why: All six findings reproduced with the attacker's programs. Findings 3 to 6 (open goals, absmodel turned off by equalities, div-trunc, ovl-ret) were already present in the baseline, which is equally slow or runs out of memory. So they are not regressions caused by FIX or FULL. They still meet the PERFORMANCE definition (more than 5 s, or a crash, under FIX or FULL, in under 40 lines), and soundness.md does not list them as known limitations, so they stay confirmed. Only findings 1 (eqsolve) and 2 (occurs) are slowdowns that the fixes themselves introduced. Ancillary claim checked: occurs-dag-16 takes 3054 ms on base and 2354 ms under FULL. That cost is in reify and predates the fixes, so it is not an occurs regression. In the eqsolve fix, place the reflexive fast path after fact collection, so that programs with quantified equality givens still get notApplicable and the result stays identical.
